title: Sununu vs. Pappas: High-Stakes Senate Race in New Hampshire
summary:
Republican John E. Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas will compete for an open U.S. Senate seat in New Hampshire in a race that has emerged as one of a handful around the country that could determine control of the chamber in November. Sununu, a former U.S. senator, and Pappas, a member of the U.S. House, are vying to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision not to seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races.

Both entered their respective party primaries as strong front-runners and now have just eight weeks to make their case to general election voters. Republicans view the seat as an opportunity to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a critical part of that effort.

In other top races, Stefany Shaheen, Shaheen's daughter, won a close primary and will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in the race to fill Pappas' open seat in the 1st Congressional District. The 2nd Congressional District will feature a matchup between U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat seeking her second term, and Republican Lily Tang Williams.

Pappas, who is giving up his seat in the 1st Congressional District after four terms, defeated four other candidates, including democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who had been gaining on him in recent weeks. Speaking to supporters at his family's restaurant in Manchester, he quickly sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu even though Sununu called him "a loser" during the 2024 presidential campaign.

"While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters," said Pappas, whose campaign also quickly posted a negative ad on social media calling Sununu "a sequel we can't afford."

"We've got to turn the page on Donald Trump's reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy and on costs, and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past," he said at his victory party.

Sununu, who defeated seven other Republicans, including former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, fired back: "He's not an independent voice for New Hampshire. Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire." Sununu's father and younger brother are both former governors, giving him deep political roots.

Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because "he never got traction back again." He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him. "I think what he's done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what's going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he's got a more stable base," Loomis said.

Stefany Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor, founded a business to help people with chronic conditions after her daughter was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She said she was campaigning to "take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs." She also emphasized healthcare, including "Medicare for all." Her opponent, Maura Sullivan, is a retired Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Obama. The race is far from over, and the outcome could have national implications.
why_it_matters: This is one of a small handful of races that will decide which party controls the entire U.S. Senate, and that balance of power affects issues young people live with, including the cost of college, health insurance rules, taxes and who gets confirmed as judges. It also shows how national battles over Trump, tariffs and Medicare for all are fought district by district in a small state like New Hampshire.

background_read: New Hampshire is a small northeastern U.S. state with famously independent voters: it hosts the country's first presidential primary, and its people often split their tickets, choosing Democrats for Congress while also electing Republican governors.

The U.S. Senate is the upper house of Congress, and only about a third of its 100 seats are contested in any given election year, which is why a race in a small state can be among the handful that decides which party controls the chamber.
Jeanne Shaheen, the senator leaving her seat, is a Democrat and a former governor of New Hampshire who has been a dominant presence in the state's politics for decades.

Her would-be successors come from two politically connected families: John E. Sununu (a Republican who previously represented New Hampshire in the Senate, and whose father and younger brother both served as the state's governor) and Chris Pappas (a Democrat who represents the state's 1st Congressional District, which includes Manchester, in the U.S. House).

National parties watch such races closely because control of the Senate shapes everything from confirming judges to passing budgets, and open seats are rare chances to flip a state from one party to the other.

perspectives.description: For Republicans and Sununu supporters, a win would give the GOP a rare Senate seat in New England and help the party keep or regain the majority. Sununu's family brand, with a father and brother who both governed New Hampshire, gives him a base of trust that can matter more than national party labels in an independent-minded state.

For Democrats and Pappas supporters, this seat is essential to their math for retaking the Senate. They argue Sununu's alliance with Trump, despite once calling Trump a loser, proves he will support corporate-friendly policies that hurt Granite State families; Pappas says a Sununu win would be a sequel the state cannot afford.

New Hampshire is a textbook swing state, and open seats in a closely divided Senate are heavily leveraged: only about a third of Senate seats are up every two years, so individual races carry outsized national weight. Because Sununu has been out of office for years and Pappas is giving up a safe House seat, both candidates carry real risks, and the national mood may decide more than local records.

The winner will help set the Senate's agenda for at least the next two years, from budget fights to judicial confirmations. With eight weeks of campaigning left, the big open questions are whether Sununu's distance from Washington reads as experience or as being out of touch, and whether Pappas can convince voters that a Democrat from Manchester, not a Sununu from a famous family, is the true independent voice for New Hampshire.
